At the event, the City announced its annual Heritage Tree selection, which strives to increase awareness and appreciation for Piedmont’s rich urban forest. The first selection was a Eucalyptus Tree in Piedmont Park near the top of Bushy Dell Creek. It was nominated by Dick Carter on behalf of the Walking on Wednesdays group. The second selection was a group of three live oaks that currently form an arc at the top of the path to Piedmont Park from Wildwood Avenue near Wildwood School. Discussions about the FY 2024-2025 budget formally began on Monday, April 15, at a special workshop before the regularly scheduled City Council meeting, though the council’s study sessions on the subject began as early as March. The current schedule of remaining meetings is as follows: • Tuesday, May 14, 6 p.m.: Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee meeting • Monday, June 3, 6 p.m.: Budget Public Hearing – City Council meeting • Monday, June 17, 6 p.m.: Adoption of the FY 2024- 2025 City budget – City Council meeting The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee’s meeting on Tuesday, May 14 will be held in the city’s Emergency Operations Centere (EOC), as is normally the case. The earlier start to the process this year indicates the City’s move towards longer-term planning, a shift that has been underway for several years at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. articles.text: Photo by Kid Vicious PR Piedmonter Mike Rufo has released a new song in honor of Earth Day 2024. Mike Rufo, a Piedmont resident and singer-songwriter, has released a new song called “The Reckoning” in honor of Earth Day 2024. Rufo’s percussive acoustic guitar number, released independently on the singer’s website and on YouTube and Spotify, combines his twin passions for music and climate activism in this meditation on society’s relationship with the environment. The song and video were released on April 19, three days before Earth Day. “The Reckoning speaks to the poignancy and power of humanity facing itself, as well as the climate crisis,” according to a press release. “Part awakening, part confessional, part plea, the song conveys the layers of emotion underlying this moment in human history as we seek to re-understand and reshape our relationship to our fragile planetary home.” Brady Blade (Indigo Girls, Emmylou Harris, Steve Earle) plays drums on the track, and Sarah Larkin (The Real Sarahs) provides vocals. “The Reckoning” is the first single from Rufo’s new album, Living Is. The album, his fourth LP, will be released in late 2024 with a series of monthly singles preceding it. Other musicians have given Rufo’s previous album, Helsinki, positive reviews. “The part of my musical consciousness that was nurtured by the likes of Simon & Garfunkel [...] donned a warm smile while listening to Mike Rufo’s recent album, Helsinki,” said Gaelynn Lea, the American violinist who won NPR’s Tiny Desk Contest in 2016. “The melodies are lovely, the lyrics straightforward and honest, and the guitar rings true - beautiful, clear, and unpretentious.” In addition to his musical career, Rufo is an energy-climate policy consultant and a board member of Music Declares Emergency (MDE), an environmental advocacy organization. Mike has directed several sustainable energy consultancies and received a Lifetime Achievement Award for his contributions to sustainable energy programs and policies. For more information on “The Reckoning,” visit www.mikerufomusic.com.

articles.text: Piedmont firefighters led by Capt. Justin McNulty (left), Brittany Borges, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, and Anthony Renteria hold last year’s trophies from the 2003 Big Climb. Along with Firefighters Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, and Brian Protheroe, Piedmont Fire will attempt to defend their first-place title this year. The Piedmont Fire Department will compete against other Bay Area fire departments in this year’s Big Climb on Saturday, May 4, as part of the First Responder Challenge, a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The event is a competitive race up a series of stairs at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. Participants will compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s entrance on Second Street. Last year, Piedmont won the first responder division in both the team and individual categories. They will have to defend their title this year as they go against the fire departments from San Francisco, San Mateo, and others. “We’ve done a lot of different fitness things over the years, whether it was CrossFit competitions or the Firefighter Challenge, which is an agility course,” explained Capt. Justin McNulty. “This competition came up last year for the first time when a local resident suggested it to us.” McNulty was the obvious choice to lead the Piedmont team. A self-described “fitness nut,” he regularly competes in physical competitions on his own time, including several running and CrossFit challenges each year. McNulty has also gained a reputation within his department for fitness running the annual 5K Piedmont Turkey Trot in full turnout gear at least half a dozen times. “I even had them change out my air bottle at the top of the hill on Sea View before I finished the course,” he told the Post. Last year marked the first time the Big Climb included a First Responders division, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. “I might be a little biased being with San Francisco Fire, but currently we’re the best at the stair climbs,” said San Francisco Fire Captain Jonathan Baxter in a promotional video. “I remember hearing that last year and thinking, ‘You don’t know what you’re doing, guys. You’re poking the bear,’” joked McNulty. The Piedmont team this year will include McNulty, Brittany Borges, Nikolas Christ, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Anthony Renteria, and Nadder Shehadeh. Erica Melgarejo, an event organizer with the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society explained that the First Responder Challenge is a great way for her organization to increase participation in its events, as well as inspire competition among departments for a good cause. “In the future, we hope to have even more departments join us at Big Climb in SF alongside other competitors to help take down blood cancer,” she explained. As of this week, Piedmont Fire Department ranks seventh in fundraising under the “corporate donor” category with $1,650. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco and to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. The Big Climb will take place this Saturday, May 4, at Oracle Park.

articles.text: On Wednesday, April 24, during the school board meeting, Piedmont High added Dr. David Yoshihara to the top of its faculty list, as the new principal. Yoshihara was selected for his nearly 30 year career in education taking him in and out of every kind of school, with an abundance of roles and titles. “Dr. Yoshihara has served in all types of schools and districts, including districts very similar in high achievement to PUSD,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. After receiving a thorough introduction from Hawn, Yoshihara, stepped to the podium in City Hall and made his first declarations in Piedmont. “I have no doubt that we will achieve great things together. Thank you once again for this incredible opportunity. Let’s make this next school year one to remember. Go Highlanders!” said Yoshihara. Yoshihara’s career shows employment in unified districts, elementary districts, high school districts, and county offices of education. Yoshihara is currently the Assistant Principal of Frick United Academy of Language in Oakland, where Superintendent Hawn, recently stopped by to have a look around. ”I also took the additional step Principal Yoshihara has a BA in Electrical Engineering from UC Berkeley, a Master of Arts from Chapman and a Doctorate from the University of La Verne. of conducting a site visit, which is not typical, but I really wanted to see Dr. Yoshihara in action with students. ‘How is he with kids?’ That’s a big question,” said Hawn. After getting to see him in action with staff and students, Hawn also talked to former board members that worked with him when he was a Superintendent in Marin County. “In all, Dr. Yoshihara shined as a collaborative leader who prioritizes relationships and building teams in the best interest of students and staff,” she concluded Some of Yoshihara’s major accomplishments include the formation of a first-of-its-kind music immersion program and the establishment of school-based wellness centers. “Your answers were extremely thoughtful and, there’s a little bit of a sense of humor, which I totally appreciate, especially stepping into a principal position at a high school,” said board member Hilary Cooper. “I just really felt like you are going to be able to connect with our students,” she added. A Piedmont welcome would not be complete without the comments of nine year board member Cory Smegal, in which, she hinted at Piedmont’s “hands-on” temperament. “The one thing to note, Piedmont High (and all of our schools) is a really important part of the community. So not only will you have support and questions from parents and students, the entire community kind of likes to be involved,” said Smegal. On July 1, Yoshihara will become PHS’s third principal in the last four years. And for Principal Yoshihara- will it be another stop on a long tour, or will Yoshihara make PHS his home?
articles.title: David Yoshihara jumps to the helm as PHS Principal

articles.text: Piedmont School District announced on April 24 the hiring of Jean Fagin as the new Director of Special Education. Fagin has experience in both rural and urban settings, from the Navajo reservation in Arizona to the cities of Chicago and Oakland. . “I am really honored and excited to step into this role in Piedmont. I will enter this work as a listener and collaborator,” said Fagin at the April 24 school board meeting. “In all, Jean shined through as the person we are looking for here in PUSD. We put her through an extensive third round interview as well. I think we grilled her for about an hour. Jean is the unicorn that we were looking for,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Fagin has a 22-year career in special education, 14 of which were spent in the classroom. She replaces outgoing Director of SPED Douglas Harter, who held the position for three years. “Jean’s initial training was focused on teaching students with moderate to severe disabiliJean Fagin was selected as Director of Special Education by an interview panel that included teachers, program specialists, school board members, community members, parents and students. ties, but she has also worked with students with a wide range of abilities, including as a Resource Teacher, co-teacher, and Special Day Class teacher,” said Hawn. Fagin earned her undergraduate degree and certification from Illinois State University and her graduate degree from Loyola University in Chicago. She will officially take over on July 1.

articles.text: Piedmont students take on another Mock Trial team during the 2024 Mock Trial California finals. Piedmont High’s Mock Trial team advanced to the State Finals in Los Angeles on March 22 as the representative for Alameda County. Piedmont finished in 12th place out of 32 County winners from across California. “I am incredibly proud of the team,” said team advisor Hillary Freeman. “It was so exciting to watch them compete at this level, place twelfth in the state and take home two outstanding witness awards. This achievement is a testament to their talent, dedication, hard work and exemplary teamwork throughout the season.” Round one action began in the Stanley Mosk Courthouse on Friday afternoon. Piedmont’s Defense team was in the courtroom first to compete against the prosecution team of Redwood High School. While nearly the entire Piedmont team made the trip south, some members were delayed in Piedmont to compete for their lacrosse team Friday afternoon. “Defense getting selected for the first round on Friday was definitely not ideal. Since we had a ton of athletes who were coming to Los Angles late, lots of people had to substitute, mostly alternates and members of the prosecution team.” explained PHS Mock Trial President Jane Hempeck. Although in unfamiliar roles, Piedmont students won their first match with Redwood High School of Tulare County. “We were definitely nervous, but the team did an amazing job, and beat our opponents even with little practice of the material,” said Hempeck. The scoring system used in the state finals is confusing, if not opaque. Scoring is based on power rankings and power matches and each trial has three judges who submit ballots in favor of the prosecution or defense. In the second round, now as a prosecution team, Piedmont won again by beating Yolo County’s Da Vinci Charter. In the third round, the Highlanders battled a familiar foe, Mt. Tamalpais. “We were really excited; we had scrimmaged them in the fall. Both teams were extremely well prepped,” said Freeman. In the state finals Piedmont lost to Tamalpais High on a split decision, 2-1. “We were nervous going against Tam. They’re a super impressive team and have won State the past few years. It definitely taught us a lot about performance, but we did awesome. I think the round was pretty close,” said Hempeck. Tamalpais went on to win all its matches and finished in 3rd place, narrowly missing the finals. Trinity Pacific Christian from Ventura County defeated Torrey Pines in the finals and will represent the state of California in the national competition, May 2-5 in Delaware. In Piedmont’s 4th match, they went against a top notch team, Menlo School from Atherton. They gained some points but ended up losing and Menlo finished in 10th place. “I don’t think Mock Trial is a widely known activity, and so seeing that there were so many others who also participate across the state was cool. Our team really rose to the challenge, and performed to the standard that we’ve been striving for since September,” said Piedmont senior and Mock Trial member Elena Stevens. PHS History teacher Hillary Freeman led the Mock Trial team to state in her first year as Mock Trial Faculty Advisor. Unlike in earlier years, the team did not have a parent attorney as advisor. PHS Mock Trial defeated Bishop O’Dowd on February 29 to secure the Alameda County title and earn them this trip to the state finals. Piedmont’s Mock Trial team competes in the state finals in Los Angeles’ Stanley Mosk Courthouse.

articles.text: As spring break began on April 6, ten Piedmont Middle School students and their families boarded an overnight flight to Havana, Cuba, loaded down with baseball gear and eager to experience legendary Cuban baseball. “We were just 90 miles from Florida,” said Carolyn Stewart, mother of seventh grader Aidan Stewart. “But as soon as we stepped off the plane, we felt like we were a world away.” The Piedmont families were in awe of the unfamiliar sights, streets full of classic cars, oncegrand mansions crumbling into the sea and endless images of Che Guevara. But it was at the baseball field at Santiago “Changa” Maderos stadium where the magic of the trip happened. The Piedmont team played four baseball games on successive days with competitive Cuban teams. While interpreters helped bridge the language barrier between umpires, coaches and players, the kids quickly realized that everyone spoke the universal language of baseball. Five Cuban 14-year-old players joined the Piedmont team and friendships formed quickly as everyone seamlessly became teammates. The opponents’ families displayed a taste of Latin American sports fandom with lively chants and cheering and a very distinct horn that blared loudly from their side of the stadium. It was their first double win since 2017. Lucas Smolko took home the singles championship with a 6-2, 6-2 win over Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai, while Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won 6-2, 7-6 (7-3) over O’Dowd’s Elias Cross and Max Hamilton for the doubles title. “I can’t remember the last time we won two championships, let alone be in both finals,” coach Jim Landes said on Saturday. Smolko appeared in last year’s finals as a freshman against San Leandro’s Elijah Cho, but lost in three sets. This year, he received a first-round bye with the top seed before shutting out Castro Valley’s Arik Hoffman 6-0, 6-0 in the second round. He then beat Berkeley’s Sze Ting Chen in the semifinals 6-3, 6-3. Smolko lost to Chen in straight sets on March 20, but defeated Chen 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 recently on April 18. In Saturday’s match, Smolko played with consistency and beat Chen with long rallies. “The first match, he really brought it to me with big serves and big forehands. articles.text: 8-7 win over rival O’Dowd; PHS gets No. 5 seed in NCS playoffs Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got the job done in the 2024 Western Alameda County Conference tournament by beating league rival Bishop O’Dowd 8-7 on April 26. In a game played at Berkeley High, the win marked the team’s first league title since 2019 To get there, PHS defeated No. 4 Newark Memorial 19-2 in the semifinals. They have qualified for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs and will be the No. 5 seed. It was a fitting championship victory over O’Dowd, which won the last two league titles. Piedmont had to respond to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but the Highlanders quickly responded with goals by Friedie Schickedanz and Ruby Guzdar. “Part of it is we were getting very frustrated. I told them we have to clean up some things like dropped balls, turnovers, and making really good decisions. We kept the plays very simple; possession, possession, possession,” coach Carlton Chan said. PHS dominated O’Dowd 15-3 on March 22, but the Dragons were without star player Lucy Yu, a junior who gas already committed to Cornell, She is the daughter of former PHS championship-winning boys’ lacrosse coach Al Yu. A big part Ruby Guzdar scoring one of her four goals against Bishop O’Dowd. Friedie Schickedanz scored twice on Bishop O’Dowd. of the finals game on Friday was shutting down Yu with speedy defender Hailey Marshburn shadowing her for the entire game. PHS consistently pressed Yu to force her around the top of the 12-meter fan. “Basically, I had to apply pressure and make sure she didn’t get the ball. But it’s hard knowing she’s a Div. 1 commit as a junior,” said Marshburn “I just tried to get in front of her because we knew she’d try to drive to the right. It was all about communication,”. It was a big game for goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter, who had 12 saves. “Lucy is so fast. We had two or three people on her at a time,” Hattan-Kutter said. “I have to say, Annika had one of her best games of the entire season. She kept us in the game,” Chan said. With five minutes left in the game, Chan made a similar call to their 2019 North Coast Section title, which was an identical 8-7 win over San Marin. “Leep possession and kill the clock,” he told the team in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s attack ate away the final five minutes of the game, largely with Guzdar and Schickedanz quickly changing possession, while Guzdar used her speed to evade multiple defenders. “We killed the clock in our Berkeley game. Against Miramonte, they scored late and won it in overtime, and that was heartbreaking. Friedie and I knew we weren’t going to give it up. It was so stressful, the main thing was to just keep the ball,” Guzdar said.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team showcased exceptional talent and determination at the West Alameda County Conference championships on Friday, April 26 at Chabot College in Hayward. Piedmont’s athletes delivered outstanding performances, including the boys’ team winning the event and the girls’ team claiming second place. The boys achieved a remarkable milestone, winning the meet for the first time in 15 years. PHS emerged as the top medal earner among all 12 teams, amassing a total of 21 medals. They outdid Berkeley’s 19 medals and Castro Valley’s 15. Coach Colby Price commended the team’s performance, noting the challenges posed er teams with greater numbers. “Bigger teams gobbled up points in events where we just don’t have the numbers,” Price said of the girls placing second. ”Those teams are double our numbers in size, but the talent of our girls team always shines bright enough to stay in the mix, we just need more numbers to get all the way to the top.” Boys’ highlights Owen Blanford won two events on the day. He was first of 27 in the 500 freestyle in 4:40.98, while he won the 200 Free in 1:42.74 out of 35 swimmers. Cole Carnazzo also won a pair of events. He won the 100 Breast in 59.43 in a field of 45 swimmers and won the 100 Fly in 52.42 against a field of 26. Dima Secor won the 200 Individual Medley in 2:00.21 against 19 other swimmers. He won his event by 8.45 seconds over the next best swimmer. Asher Takazawa won his 100 backstroke in 54.22 against 33 swimmers. The 400 Free relay team of Blanford, Takazawa, Tom Rolefson and Nik Costello won against 24 other teams, clocking a time of 3:14.53. They beat the next best team by 6.7 seconds. articles.text: After rain rescheduled their third race, Piedmont High School and Piedmont Devo (junior development) mountain biking teams raced their third race of the season with the NorCal NiCA League in Granite Bay on the beach of Folsom Lake in Folsom, CA on Sunday April 28. Due to rescheduling, the race was set for the morning after Senior Prom, meaning Piedmont only brought a group of six high school riders. The course at Granite Bay was fast with a mixture of single track through meadows, forest, sandy beach terrain, and a few muddy puddles. Each lap is 6.2 miles with 576 feet of vertical gain. JV races two laps, while Varsity and JV1 race three laps. Varsity rider Max Rivera proved his dedication, finishing his 18 mile race with a time of 1:20:47, placing 31st and advancing in points. Olive Reining, a sophomore, racing on the JV2 Girls team, had her strongest race of the season by finishing in front of some familiar rivals with a time of 1:25:30. Caleb Canada and Asher Villareal, sophomores, raced next in the JV2 Boys race. Caleb came in with a very strong result of 1:04:23 finishing 21st out 34. Asher persevered through the rising heat and brought it in with a time of 1:21:59. Jasper Schuetz and Cary Ward raced for the JV1 boys team when the sun was at full blast. This exciting race was off to a quick start with Jasper leading a pack of six riders around the first lap in what was nicknamed the “Pain Train.” On the second lap he was third approaching the lap line but advanced in the sand on the beach to be right behind the lead, averaging 270 watts. The top three kept trading places throughout the third and final lap with Jasper putting in a final effort of 1200 watts for 15 seconds at the finish to beat Casey Warren of Berkeley High School by 0.5 seconds. His time was 1:12:57. This win brings Jasper into contention for winning the series, pending the results of his final race of the season on May 11th. Sunday was a redeeming win for Schuetz, responding strongly from placing 12th in his first race of the season due to a cold, while he placed second in his most recent race. articles.text: Free event includes kid-friendly museum-curated art activities de Youngsters Day Out invites Bay Area kids to engage with deYoung Museum’s permanent collections through hands-on activities. Visit the de Young Museum this Saturday, May 4, to experience de Youngsters Day Out, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s annual free community day for children. Family-friendly activities will be led by de Young’s teaching artists, allowing children to engage with the museum’s permanent collections through hands-on activities. The event also raises funds for arts education through the Equity School Partnership Project, an initiative with the San Francisco and Oakland Unified School Districts that provides art education to students in the Bay Area. “We are delighted to bring the de Youngsters Day Out to the families of the Bay Area,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Not only does this annual event provide crucial funding for our Equity School Partnership Project, but it also opens up museum doors to a new generation of visitors and connects them with art through a range of engaging activities. It’s a joy to see our galleries come alive with the creativity and excitement of children.” Activities include the San Francisco Public Library’s “Library on Wheels,” a mobile library program that gives out free reading materials for children and parents, as well as free eye exams by Zenni Eyewear. De Youngsters Day Out begins at 10 a.m. and will remain open until 5:15 p.m. with event activities wrapping up at 4 p.m. No registration is required. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will exhibit Art of Noise, on view May 4 through August 18, to showcase groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise will feature over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. articles.text: Blue Door, Tanya Barfield’s new two-man play, premieres on the Aurora Theatre Company stage in Berkeley this Friday, April 19. Barfield’s play features Lewis, a high-achieving Black mathematics professor, in conversation with three generations of his ancestors during a sleepless night as he wrestles with his own sense of self and cultural identity. Lewis is estranged from his white wife, who accuses him of being out of touch with his heritage for refusing to attend the Million Man March, a grassroots demonstration of African-American men in Washington, D.C., on October 16, 1995. At that time, organizers united in self-help and self-defense against economic and social ills plaguing their communities. The ancestral visitations Lewis receives call upon joy and pain as well as music and song to situate him in a long lineage of Black men in America from enslavement and Jim Crow to Black Power. articles.text: A scene from Mark Morris Dance Company’s production of Socrates Always count on the dean of US modern-dance choreographers, Mark Morris, 67, to pull rabbits out of the hat. The company director lost none of his mojo when he moved from dance toward theater pieces. The Mark Morris Dance Group performed a rarity at Zellerbach Hall. Not only was MM’s Via Dolorosa a world premiere, but it was the first time in memory that the veteran ever tackled a sacred-religious theme in dance with his troupe. His dancers – nine of them here, all stellar interchangeable parts – are exquisitely disciplined, with a unique lightness of foot, bobbing weightlessly about stage, playing out the Passion of Jesus Christ in rather abstract fashion. I’d even use that word taboo among dance reviewers, “graceful.” Christ was sometimes male, sometimes female. And various underplayed images caught the moment, whether crowds pointing fingers accusingly at prisoner Christ, or a dancer with arms outstretched portrayed Jesus crucified, or the whole group falling gently to the floor to portray his death. This was MM playing the supreme classicist, going way back to Biblical references subtly alluded to, with a deft, sprightly corps to show classical dance modes with a minimum of finery or décor, apart from Howard Hodgkin’s blazing/colorful abstract backdrops. This unusual 40-minute venture into sacred dance was backed by one mere solo harp (Parker Ramsay) rather than a Bach Passion or Verdi Requiem pounded out by an orchestra. To quote the architect Mies van der Rohe, “Less is more.” One resounding boo had pepPhoto by Chris Hardy pered the dance group’s opening night, possibly reacting to the Christ theater piece, with all the walking and stylized reenactments in place of, well, dance. But we still call it the MM Dance Group, no?? A companion piece on the program was Morris’ Socrates (2010). This work leaned heavily on painted images on ancient Greek vases, portrayed in two-dimensional fashion by the 15 dancers. Exquisite lightness of foot once again, but without the Satie music for solo piano and tenor (in incomprehensible French). You’d never know it had anything to do with the great ancient-Greek philosopher, his condemnation and his death scene. MARK MORRIS DANCE GROUP in two works by the director/choreographer Morris. Cal Performances, Zellerbach Hall, Berkeley, CA, April 19-20. For info: (510) 642-9988, or go online www.calperformances.org.

articles.text: Premiere of award-winning show is this Sunday, May 5 Berkeley Repertory Theatre will premiere the award-winning play Galileo this Sunday, May 5. Historically, Alexander the Great defeated the Persians, but he admired Persian culture big time. I am willing to bet that Alexander enjoyed ancient Persian cuisine. That premise started an adventure. Some cuisines offer consistency, some offer variety, and some offer value. I discovered that Persian cuisine offers some challenges. Some of the Persian restaurants I tried in the past are simply not very interesting. Alborz, in Berkeley is head and shoulders above the average. The food is beautiful in service and in preparation. Portions are large, and to top it off, the service is gracious and attentive. Finally, the prices are reasonable. Is this the result of 3,000 years of culture? As our group of four arrived at Alborz, we immediately noticed the lovely ambience. The staff is mostly Mexican though the owners are Persian. For the cuisine… Your server can advise you. articles.text: Babou Ceesay and Helen Mirren in Eye in the Sky In many ways the well-made and superbly acted Eye in the Sky is reassuring. But it can also be chillingly disconcerting. At the outset we see a straightforward surveillance of a militant group associated with the East Africa terrorist organization Al Shabab. It then unexpectedly morphs into something far more serious and morally hazardous. What is initially being watched from an altitude of 20,000 feet by an unseen, eerily quiet drone is a house in Nairobi, Kenya, where a meeting is taking place between highly placed Shabab leaders, to include a woman, a British citizen, who has aligned herself with the organization. The original plan is to raid the house and capture those inside. But using a cyborg beetle, an agent (Barkhad Abdi, who starred in the film Captain Phillips), is sitting outside on the street and using a control no larger than a cell phone. He positions the small beetle with a miniaturized camera inside the house where it reveals that in another room several suicide bombers are preparing to put on explosive vests. The stakes have suddenly changed for all concerned – Col. Katherine Powell (Helen Mirren), located in Surrey England, and Lt. General Frank Benson (Alan Rickman), who is in London with several British ministers and politicians. What was a “capture” is now suddenly reframed as a “kill.” The only question, both legal and moral, is what will be the collateral damage once the drone releases its hellfire missile. Complicating that question is the presence of a small girl, seated just outside the house at a table where she sells her mother’s homemade flatbread to passing locals. She is clearly within the kill zone. The pilot of the drone (Aaron Paul) remarkably is in Nevada. When he spots the girl he asks for a review of all facets of the operation, to include legal and ethical concerns. And so the tension is continually ratcheted up. Powell and Benson argue that to delay could mean that the suicide bombers will leave and ultimately appear in a shopping mall where perhaps hundreds of innocents will be maimed or killed. This reality is weighed against the life of that one little girl. Others argue for delay as the decision is “referred up.” No civilian in the room with the General Benson wants to take final responsibility. Across four continents, involving ministers and secretaries of state, the “kill” decision is incrementally postponed. The reality that confronts those involved, to include the pilot of the drone, is the proverbial rock and the hard place. The debate is both agonizing and complex and riveting. What is done is done in the name of the British and the American people. Collateral damage is a euphemism that is laden with horrible, unintended consequences. And to make the moment even more dreadful is that it has a video game quality to it – warfare at its most detached. This is an intense and rare military meditation on war that focuses not on the battle but on the choices that we ask our military personnel to make as they conduct this most lethal form of warfare. To its credit the film avoids becoming a melodrama, while still examining effectively the moral quandary that we can only hope our soldiers and officials confront with each “kill” order. Eye in the Sky is taut and well constructed and highly recommended. Eye in the Sky. Directed by Gavin Hood. Starring Helen Mirren, Aaron Paul and Alan Rickman. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated R. Released in 2016, Streaming on prime/MAX/apple tv.

articles.text: Winston Churchill once said, “Democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the others that have been tried.” And because democracy is collaboration, a process of advise and consent executed by human beings, it is deeply flawed. Too often democracy means governance by narrow, self-serving men and women who are ruled by the principles of careers, mendacity and venality. Many are also incompetent. And messy offers fertile ground for satire, as demonstrated in the British film In the Loop, a high energy, over-the-top send-up about the period leading up to the invasion of Iraq (though Iraq is never mentioned). Good satire can be difficult to achieve, often reliant on biting humor, ridicule, and irony. The air can often take leave of the satirical balloon and it can quickly fall into absurdity and silliness. In the Loop doesn’t, due to its staccato-like writing, with smart lines dropped like cluster bombs. It is both bitingly funny and scarily accurate. Britain ministers and directors of communication, in collusion with American undersecretaries and their sycophants, fashion a Baroque rationale for war, created out of whole cloth, based on unimpeachable intelligence, derived from a Middle East source, code name The Iceman. It’s a house of cards, pure fiction, reconstructed to resemble truth. No matter, apparently, that both British and American soldiers will be put in harm’s way and irrevocable actions will result in blood and treasure being expended. Recall the United Nations presentation by General Colin Powell, pointing to weapons of mass destruction on a split screen high above the Chamber of Nations, and the ubiquitous color-coded alerts perpetrated by an administration that was the purveyor of fear and catastrophe at every political turn. This is not to say that In the Loop has a light touch or is subtle. It’s a wonderfully blunt instrument, beginning with a bevy of Anglo-Saxon epithets, plumbed to great effect and delivered with practiced hostility by the Prime Minister’s communication director, Malcom Tucker (Peter Capaldi). Capaldi’s portrayal is but one example of a host of English and American actors who give nifty performances, each convincing. It’s hard not to think of the Kabuki dance being played out today in Washington around healthcare. Like war, the stakes are high, and yet the dissembling scenarios, the theatrical town hall meetings, complemented by wingnuts packing heat, all make In the Loop timeless and prescient. In the Loop is satire at its best: thought-provoking, exaggerated and delightfully humorous. In The Loop. Directed by Armando Iannucci. Starring Tom Hollander, Peter Capaldi, James Gandolfini, and Gina McKee. 1 hr., 46 min. Not rated. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv. articles.text: To begin with, kids are going to enjoy a Bug’s Life. It’s a superb, animated feature filled with a creepy-crawly menagerie of bugs, inspired by an Aesop’s Fable titled The Ant and the GrasshopThe story opens with a wonderfully natural-looking colony of ants that makes its home on a mound of dirt, near a creek bed. It’s known as Ant Island and is ruled by the Queen ant and her daughter, Princess Atta (Julia As we soon learn, every summer a gang of thuggish grasshoppers arrive, led by the swaggering Hopper (Kevin Spacey), and they demand to be given food collected by the hard-working colony. A nerdy ant named Flik (Dave Foley), a young tinkerer, has an accident while trying to invent a conveyor belt to move the seeds intended for the grasshoppers. When the gadget malfunctions, he knocks the gathered food into the water. Whoops. Hopper is furious, and he demands that the ants give him twice as much food as promised, to make up for the loss. Flik, rebelling, feeling bullied, insists that the demand for double the rations is wrong, and suggests to the Queen that he be allowed to leave and find bigger bugs, warrior types, to help the colony in a fight against the grasshoppers. Enough is enough. Princess Atta, apparently not a fan of Flik, encourages him, assuming it’s unlikely that he will return from his mission. Flik journeys to Bug City (a heap of trash piled under a trailer), and it’s there that he recruits a cohort of “warriors” who are actually a troupe of Circus Bugs that had recently been fired by ringmaster P.T. Flea (John Ratzenberger). The group agrees to return to Ant Hill with Flik, who they think is a talent scout, having no idea what they are getting into. When they arrive at the colony, they discover what is afoot and that they are not there to perform. Flik pleads with them to stay and pretend to be what they’re not: fightA STEINWAY Teaching Partner Superpower of the Song™ by Kadie Kelly Piano lessons + / Sound Healing experiences I was drawn to the piano, singing and composing music from an early age. Throughout my life, music has been a source of happiness, community, self-expression and healing. My background is rooted in classical music, but I also have experience with pop music, leadsheets, blues, song-writing, and singing. I have always sought out collaborations with people with diverse musical experiences to gain new perspectives and skills, and I pass that affinity and curiosity on to my students. I value self determination, and in supporting students in the needs that they have, where they are.

articles.text: Further adventures with Antonio Banderas Kids will thoroughly enjoy Dreamworks’ sequel Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. It’s been more than a decade since the release of the popular Puss in Boots, so perhaps it would be helpful to begin with the first animated feature as a good way to introduce the young ones to Puss, the swashbuckling, daring feline. The narrative begins when Puss (Antonio Banderas), never risk averse, realizes his escapades have used up eight of his allotted nine lives. Listening to his doc’s advice, he decides to retire and live a more domestic life. pages.text: Wednesday, May 1, 2024 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS A Bug’s Life – a delight for kids Puss in Boots: The Last Wish Further adventures with Antonio Banderas By Chris Honoré Kids will thoroughly enjoy Dreamworks’ sequel Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. It’s been more than a decade since the release of the popular Puss in Boots, so perhaps it would be helpful to begin with the first animated feature as a good way to introduce the young ones to Puss, the swashbuckling, daring feline. The narrative begins when Puss (Antonio Banderas), never risk averse, realizes his escapades have used up eight of his allotted nine lives. Listening to his doc’s advice, he decides to retire and live a more domestic life. He hangs up his boots and sword, and tries to commit to simply hanging out with the old cat lady, Mama Luna (Da’Vine Joy Randolph). Of course he grows restless. When he finds himself standing in a long line to use the litter box, he knows there has to be a better alternative. Boots comes to the realization that if he is going to succeed in his quest he will need help. He hooks up with his former partner, Kitty Soft Paws (Salma Hayek). Reluctantly they agree to take along the annoying, endlessly talking Perrito (Harvey Guillén). We see a panoply of familiar fairytale characters such as the Three Bears, Little Jack Horner See The Last Wish on page 31 By Chris Honoré To begin with, kids are going to enjoy a Bug’s Life. It’s a superb, animated feature filled with a creepy-crawly menagerie of bugs, inspired by an Aesop’s Fable titled The Ant and the Grasshopper. The story opens with a wonderfully natural-looking colony of ants that makes its home on a mound of dirt, near a creek bed. It’s known as Ant Island and is ruled by the Queen ant and her daughter, Princess Atta (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). As we soon learn, every summer a gang of thuggish grasshoppers arrive, led by the swaggering Hopper (Kevin Spacey), and they demand to be given food collected by the hard-working colony. A nerdy ant named Flik (Dave Foley), a young tinkerer, has an accident while trying to invent a conveyor belt to move the seeds intended for the grasshoppers. When the gadget malfunctions, he knocks the gathered food into the water. Whoops. Hopper is furious, and he demands that the ants give him twice as much food as promised, to make up for the loss. Flik, rebelling, feeling bullied, insists that the demand for double the rations is wrong, and suggests to the Queen that he be allowed to leave and find bigger bugs, warrior types, to help the colony in a fight against the grasshoppers. Enough is enough. Princess Atta, apparently not a fan of Flik, encourages him, assuming it’s unlikely that he will return from his mission. Flik journeys to Bug City (a heap of trash piled under a trailer), and it’s there that he recruits a cohort of “warriors” who are actually a troupe of Circus Bugs that had recently been fired by ringmaster P.T. Flea (John Ratzenberger). The group agrees to return to Ant Hill with Flik, who they think is a talent scout, having no idea what they are getting into. When they arrive at the colony, they discover what is afoot and that they are not there to perform. articles.text: Wondering how to attract beautiful butterflies and buzzing bees to your garden? It all begins with growing native plants. Traditional gardens are often about displaying control over nature, which is the exact opposite of what wildlife wants. By providing a safe place to eat and nest, gardeners can support the pollination role that native bees, butterflies, and birds play in the garden. In return you’ll get a front row seat to the wonders of nature. It’s important to grow native plants because they’ve evolved alongside the wildlife there. Let’s take the most famous duo as an example, Monarch butterflies and Milkweed. Milkweed is not only the host plant that Monarchs lay their eggs on, but it’s also the food source that their caterpillars have evolved to digest. A prime reason why we have to support pollinators for their whole life cycle. If you’re ready to get growing, here is UC Davis Arboretum’s short list of easy to grow native plants for the East Bay: • Ray Hartman California lilac • California poppy • Catmint • Russian sage • Germander sage • Cascade Creek goldenrod • California Milkweed Each of these plants provides an excellent source of pollen for a variety of native bees and butterflies. To find these plants, visit Annie’s Annuals in Richmond or Native Here Nursery in Berkeley’s Tilden Park for all your East Bay native plant needs. If adding more plants to your garden isn’t practical, the easiest way to help native pollinators is to let your lawn grow long in spring. No Mow May is a movement to help bring biodiversity back to our cities. Native plants will attract butteries and bees into your garden. grow longer and letting flowers bloom, we can provide a pollen source for newly emerging spring pollinators. Last year during No Mow May, I discovered a patch of native grass and ladybug larvae in my lawn. As Rebecca McMackin, Ecological Horticulturalist, puts it, “all of these practices create new looks for our gardens. But part of this work is changing our ideas of beauty.” Remember, it’s not all or nothing. There’s almost always space where we can let things grow a little wild. To learn about adding native mason bees to your garden, visit my Youtube channel Girl And Her Dog Farm. Inspired to get planting? articles.text: Member of 2004 World Series champion Boston Red Sox A loving husband and father, former MLB first baseman and outfielder David Andrew McCarty, 54, passed away suddenly and unexpectedly on April 19, 2024. Known for his versatility, fielding, and power threat off the bench, Dave had an 11-year major league career with seven teams, including the 2004 Red Sox during their historic championship season that would break the infamous “Curse of the Bambino.” Born in Houston, Texas on November 23, 1969, Dave excelled both athletically and academically at Sharpstown High School. Recruited in baseball and basketball, he decided to focus on baseball and picked “the farm” at Stanford University in California (BA ‘92), where he would meet Piedmont native Monica Canty (PHS ’85), his wife of 32 years, who was attending Stanford Law School. The two were married on January 11, 1992. While at Stanford, Dave put up record numbers that would eventually land him in the Stanford Hall of Fame, including a 1991 season with a .420 batting average, 24 homers, 66 RBI, and an incredible .828 slugging percentage. Over his college summer months, he played in the Cape Cod Baseball League (1989 Cotuit Kettleers) and for Team USA in the 1990 Baseball World Cup. An All-American and Baseball America’s College Player of the Year, Dave was the third pick in the 1991 draft by the Minnesota Twins. That marked the beginning of a 14-year journey filled with many ups and downs that would see him play for nine different baseball organizations and seven major league teams over 11 seasons. The once top prospect would become a journeyman utility player who could come off the bench to play defense, provide a power-threat, and – a few times – pitch. The 6’5” right-handed batting, left-handed throwing (an unusual combination in baseball) first baseman, nicknamed “Big Mac” by his teammates, lightened the clubhouse with his sharp humor and enjoyed razzing the pitchers about his 2.45 ERA (3.2 IP, 4 SO, 1 BB). Over his career, Dave played in 630 major league games with the Minnesota Twins (1993– 1995), Cincinnati Reds (1995), Dave McCarty with World Series trophy at Fenway Park on April 9, 2024, at a celebration of the 20th anniversary of the Red Sox World Championship Family Day at Fenway Park during the 2004 Championship season The McCarty family (Reid, Monica, Maxine and Dave) at Royal Ascot in England, June 2023 San Francisco Giants (1995– 1997), Seattle Mariners (1998), Detroit Tigers (1999), Kansas City Royals (2000–2002), Tampa Bay Devil Rays (2002), Oakland Athletics (2003), and Boston Red Sox (2003–2005), posting a career average of .242 with 36 home runs, and 175 RBIs. With a Stanford degree to fall back on, Dave was tempted to hang up his spikes many times over the years. But he stuck with it and was rewarded when he was signed by Billy Beane of the Oakland A’s in 2000 during the “Moneyball” era. It rejuvenated his career. After an exceptional Spring Training with the A’s, Dave was traded to the Royals where he had his most productive season with career highs in batting average (.278), home runs (12), RBI (68), and games played (103). But the highlight of Dave’s baseball career was being part of the 2004 Red Sox, who were dubbed “The Idiots” due to their infamously loose clubhouse and inventive facial hair. Down three games to none in the ALCS, the Sox mounted a historic comeback against the Yankees. They would go on to defeat the Cardinals in four games in the World Series, winning eight in a row and breaking the Red Sox’s 86-year championship drought. Dave retired from baseball in 2005 but continued to work for the Red Sox as an analyst on NESN until the 2008 season. Dave adjusted to life after baseball with surprising ease. He joined Lee & Associates as one of the founding members of the commercial real estate firm’s Oakland office in 2006. There he found the camaraderie that he’d missed from the clubhouse and a job that he loved. While baseball was a large part of his life, the most important thing to Dave was family. With the demanding life on the road behind him, he was able to turn his four months of being a devoted, hands-on dad into twelve. Dave and Monica moved to Piedmont, CA in 2000 to raise their two children, Reid (PHS ’15) and Maxine (PHS ’17). The same big personality, sharp wit, and easy smile that made Dave a popular figure in the clubhouse continued after he retired; he was a well-known figure around town, walking the kids to school and taking them to various activities or sport practices. The family shared a love of sports – and competition – from the ski slopes, to the swimming pool, to the golf course, to the hiking trail. Staying active was a big part of Dave’s life. The former journeymen never stopped traveling. The family explored the globe together, traveling to Russia, China, Japan, Iceland, the Baltics, Europe, Greece, Mexico, Canada, and spending many weeks a year in London. Closer to home favorite spots were Tahoe, Hawaii, and frequent trips to the Disney parks. Dave’s passing comes just weeks after he and other members of the 2004 team were honored at Fenway Park as part of the 20-year anniversary of their championship season, a fitting sendoff to a man who was a champion in both sport and life. Dave was preceded in death by his father, Dennis. He is survived by his wife, Monica, his children, Reid and Maxine, his mother, Joan, his sister, Kelly, and a large much-loved extended family. A celebration of Dave’s wonderful life will be held on Thursday May 9, 2024. More information can be found at https:// rb.gy/xr9i93. In lieu of flowers, please consider donations to Sunflower Hill in Pleasanton, CA (a special needs housing and programs community) or the Special Olympics of Northern California, where Dave and his son Reid recently won a gold medal in a local golf competition.
